utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I raise some matters very briefly at this stage

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The first concerns the French translation. Over the last three weeks or so, the Defence counsel has repeatedly raised issues in respect of the quality of the translations by the French booth. At times, the Defence counsel has risen to his feet every 10 minutes, or even more frequently, with such concerns. Yesterday evening, it reached the point that the pace of evidence slowed down to an extraordinary extent. Mr. President, it thus becomes an issue for the Prosecution when it impacts upon the ability of the Prosecution to keep to its timetable. I do not rise to my feet with a particular solution as a proposal but rather, at this stage, simply to alert the Trial Chamber to the impact that it is having. There have been some witnesses that I have taken over the last three weeks where it has been a problem as well. So I simply point that out as an issue which I think needs to be addressed. I do not, in making those comments, suggest for a minute that there is anything lacking in the quality of the French translation. Mr. President, the second issue I wish to raise concerns expert witnesses. You may recall that about three weeks ago I invited the Defence to indicate which witnesses it wished to have available for cross-examination and how long they expected they would be in cross-examination of those witnesses. At that time, I also indicated that I could not give the Trial Chamber a realistic estimate of precisely how much time was left in the Prosecution case because it may well be that some of those expert witnesses would be no more than a few minutes in chief and may reasonably be more than half an hour or an hour in cross-examination. We have already seen one instance of an expert witness being five minutes in chief and being a day in cross-examination. Might I respectfully suggest that the Defence indicates its position as to which witnesses, expert witnesses, it requires and for how long in cross-examination by, at the latest, Tuesday next week. If they do that, I will then give that required update the following day, on Wednesday. From that point on, the Trial Chamber will be fully aware of our latest precise estimate as to how much time is in the Prosecution case. By that date, we will also formally - that is by Tuesday - we will formally file our application in respect of 92 bis witnesses. I understand that the translations are due to be completed this week, if not already completed today. That is the second issue. And in so doing, I have mentioned a third issue, that is the timetable, and subject to the Defence giving us their indications by Tuesday, I will update the Trial Chamber on Wednesday. Fourthly, Mr. President, you indicated, I think earlier this week or late last week, that the sitting time for Monday may be varied to 9.30 to 4.30, I think it was, and also to the same times on Monday, the 17th of June, in which case, if it was, we would not sit the following day. I would be grateful, if you are in a position to do so, if you could advise us of the position not only in relation to this Monday but also the other two days because it impacts upon our planning of transporting witnesses to The Hague to give evidence. And it would involve the loss of a day, almost a full day, if we lost that Tuesday. Finally, Mr. President, the matter of the proposed witness for next Wednesday, Mr. Tucker. This morning I received a letter from the Defence, advising the Prosecution that they would not be ready to proceed with the witness Tucker on Wednesday because they have only just received yesterday his statement and a translation of his statement. And I think there may still be some exhibits to come in B/C/S. There are, I think, four exhibits to be tendered through the witness Pierce Tucker. Mr. President, I appreciate and sympathise with the position of the Defence. We have not stuck to the seven-day rule with Mr. Tucker. I will explain the reason. There is a lengthy statement, some 30 or 35 pages, which was not signed until the 3rd of May. It was immediately put into translation, and we received the translation back the day that we disclosed it to the Defence, which is yesterday. I provided yesterday a copy of the statement to the Defence, in English, which has marked on it the particular passages that we would lead from him in chief so as to assist the Defence to come to terms with that evidence. Much of the statement has nothing to do with Sarajevo. Although a translation has been provided of the full statement, exhibits which have nothing to do with Sarajevo and which are mentioned in the statement have not been provided. I would not anticipate that being an issue. Those exhibits primarily have to do with events in Srebrenica. So although we have provided copies of all of the exhibits which relate either directly or indirectly to this trial, we only intend to tender into evidence four of them. Mr. President, if we do not call Mr. Tucker on Wednesday at all, it may be that there is a break in the evidence. In saying that, I appreciate that a number of types I have risen to my feet and anticipated a break, but as it has transpired, the break never came about. Perhaps I should explain how I anticipate next week will go as far as witnesses are concerned. On Monday, we call Mr. Mole. We may not finish his evidence, that is cross-examination and re-examination, on Monday. Tuesday, we have Witness W. If we have not finished Mole by Tuesday, the Prosecution would seek your leave to interpose the evidence of Witness W. He is only available that day. If we have to interpose Witness W, I respectfully propose that we recall Mole at the end of the evidence of Witness W and finish him then, that is either on Tuesday or Wednesday, whenever Witness W is completed. The next witness was Tucker. After him is David Harland. He is unable to travel to be available to give evidence on the Wednesday. He is due to arrive in The Hague on Wednesday afternoon. There are some pressing, indeed, compelling personal factors, health factors with his family which preclude as an option him giving evidence on Wednesday. I won't go into those details unless I am required to and then in closed court. Mr. President, we then have General Van Baal for Friday. I should say that I anticipate Mr. Harland's evidence would take all of Thursday. By way of preparation for General Van Baal, we have alerted the translation unit to the need for interpreters in the Dutch language, that is, Dutch into B/C/S and French and English, as well as those three languages into Dutch, or at least French and English. Mr. President, that being the timetable, and mindful of the position that the Defence is in with Mr. Tucker, I respectfully propose that we call Tucker on Wednesday, but only to give his evidence in chief, and then he be recalled at a later stage in the trial to be subject to cross-examination. If anything, in my respectful submission, that better places the Defence because they have time not only to contemplate his statement and the exhibits but also a transcript of his sworn evidence in chief at their leisure. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Your observations in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few observations, Mr. President. I will be brief. Your Honours, good afternoon to begin with. I think that I was not well understood by Mr. Ierace, and I apologise. The Defence was never in favour of saying that they were traduttori, tradittori under any circumstance, and I would like to congratulate the French booth which translated thirdly by fourthly. Very good. Yesterday, we had problems. Yesterday, this was not because of the Defence but because the witness was very rapid, and then there was also another technical problem because the French booth had this problem, which it can explain. But when very important passages in the testimony are missing, it is my duty to point to that, and I am doing this only with great reservation and, of course, I overlook the minor matters, but we must react sometimes because our Tribunal is a bilingual one. And as regards the Witness Tucker, the Prosecution has not respected the deadlines. We must take note of that and it must bear the consequences. Therefore, Witness W, as we had said we would, we submitted our views on Witness Tucker and Witness W, and we would like to say that as far as Witness W is concerned, and regardless of the fact whether it is a UN official who falls under the category of the Rules, UN Rules of 1946. So I would like to mention also that the deadlines have not been respected, Mr. President, because the statements were made available much earlier than the moment that we actually received them. I am not speaking of the translations. And I think that Article 67(a) says that Prosecution has to submit as quickly as possible testimonies of witnesses. I don't think this has been done. I think that the deadline has been -- that there has been delay of two months from the moment it had this material until it submitted to us. Therefore, Witnesses W, X and Z cannot be accepted. And also with regard to Witness Tucker, the statements were made and taken a year ago and it is not natural, in a trial like this, that we keep putting off things until the very last moment, statements that are important and that makes it impossible for the Defence to work, and this by all the energy we put into this trial and our good will. We would like to make a request. It was not possible as regards the witness who we will cross-examine today. It might last as long as it was yesterday. And we did not have time enough to prepare the cross-examination with General Galic. I think that we can work until 5.00, but after that, we will not be able to be as efficient as we would like to be, and I think it would be good to stop at 5.00, 5.30, and then to continue the cross-examination later on Monday as soon as possible in the time we will need to look into the exhibits. The witness was very lengthy in his statements. He provided running testimony of about five hours, and we had to go into that material, and it is not possible for us to do this on the spot. And therefore, in order to increase our efficiency, we think that it would be good to work until 5.00, 5.30 p.m., and then continue on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Firstly, just quickly in relation to Tucker, the statement was not taken a year ago. It was taken over a series of interviews and, indeed, was not signed until the 3rd of May. My learned colleague also mentions the situation with Witnesses W, X and Z, and mentions that he has filed a response to our application for protective measures. Indeed, that is a matter I intended to raise as well, so that is a sixth matter. Of course, since Witness W is due to give his evidence on Tuesday, I would be grateful if the Trial Chamber could indicate its position, preferably today, but obviously, with respect, Mr. President, Monday. I should say that the other day my learned colleague said to you that these witnesses had been added to the witness list. I showed the Defence yesterday the relevant 65 ter summary and I don't think now there is any issue on that. In other words, there were 65 ter summaries for those witnesses filed before the trial commenced at the relevant time and at no time were they deleted from the witness list. There was some further material served on the Defence in relation to Witness W. Clearly, if there is to be a discussion of that material, it should happen in closed session. I am not aware of any other issue in relation to those three witnesses, other than the need for protective measures. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Let me just confer with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just give you at least a decision on a few issues, not all of them. The others will come after the first break, if possible, of course. First, the issue of translation. It should be, as a general rule, it should be observed that objections against the translations and the intervention to that end, of course, should be made if the translation does not enable us to follow the proceedings, and we had difficulties of this kind especially yesterday. Also, if the translation, even if it is a minor point, could cause confusion - not minor confusion but real confusion - then, of course, it is also -- it goes without explanation that the Defence not only could, but even should, interfere, I would say. On minor issues, we have small yellow papers and we could use them. What happened yesterday was that the speed, both of the examining party and of the witness, was such that it created major problems. I will take a bit more control during the continuation of the examination-in-chief, that is, I will give signs on who can speak at what moment. I tried to do it yesterday but perhaps I should explain this to the witness first. I expect that there will be less problems when cross-examined because we have the natural break between question and answer, since the questions have to be translated and the answers have to be translated. That is the first issue. As far as the time needed for cross-examination of the expert witnesses is concerned, the Chamber thinks that it is fair that the Defence gives this indication by the time suggested by the Prosecutor. As far as Witness W is concerned, of course, we will first like to see the submissions by the Defence and we will come back to that as soon as possible. As far as next Monday is concerned, and as far as Monday the 17th and Tuesday the 18th is concerned, the reasons I indicated that there might be a change is on the basis of the coordination we have with the Stakic case. I am just informed that on the 17th and the 18th, the schedule will be as planned before. That means that we will just sit at the scheduled times on the 17th and the 18th. As far as next Monday is concerned, we would have some extra time. Nevertheless, the Chamber would prefer to start at 9.00 in the morning, but we have, if necessary, a possibility either to have the break a bit earlier or to continue -- and then continue in the afternoon. It very much depends on how the examination of the witness develops, but we have a bit more room, as far as time is concerned, as we usually have when the Stakic case starts in the afternoon. On the issue of the schedule for next week, on the issue of the examination of Mr. Tucker and on the issue of a break by 5.00 today, the Chamber will consider this during the next break and we will inform the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. I will return at the beginning of the next session, if that is convenient to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, just one more thing I should say, perhaps to keep in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please wait for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will try to give its decision on Witness W, if possible, today, even if it would be just for the time being an oral decision, but of course we first have to look carefully to the submissions of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. The -- I rose to my feet a minute ago to suggest, respectfully suggest, that you might ask the witness Thomas how he would be placed if he was required to return on Monday because, at this stage, he is scheduled to fly out tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you, what do you exactly mean by how he would be placed?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What I have in mind, if you accede to the Defence request, a corollary of that is that he return on Monday for further cross-examination, and he may have some pressing personal problem - I don't know - which would present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Just inform whether he would be available on next Monday, if that would be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the alternative is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- he return at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if there is no other issue to be raised at this very moment, may I ask Mr. Usher to bring Mr. Thomas into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just want to inform you of one thing, after having conferred with my colleague. As far as the issue is concerned, the issue of timing and with regard to the expert witness, my colleague has reminded me, and quite rightly, that it seems that we received at a very late stage, so quite recently, the statements in the Serbian language, if I have understood that correctly, and as a result we haven't had the time to examine them in detail. I understand your decision and I thank you for that. But this poses a technical problem since we have to examine this matter in all our ignorance because we haven't been able to examine this in the Serbian language. And I think that this is the right of the General to be informed of this, to be aware of this. I wanted to point this out to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully accept that preparing for cross-examination needs that you are able to discuss the matters with your client. An indication of the approximate time needed for cross-examination is a different thing from the full preparation of the cross-examination itself. So, therefore, I think the Defence could also rely on its experience as experienced Defence lawyers, and that does not necessarily mean that all details of the reports have to be discussed with your client. But let's see how far you come and what information you could give to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I apologise for having you waiting outside of this courtroom for quite a while, meanwhile. The examination-in-chief will be continued by Mr. Mundis, but we experienced quite some problems yesterday as far as the speed was concerned. This is also caused by the fact that you and Mr. Mundis are speaking the same language. Although I am not a trained conductor, I nevertheless will try to indicate by hand signals to you when to stop and when to start. So if both Mr. Mundis and you, Mr. Thomas, would apart from -- look at me so that you can follow my indications, that would be highly appreciated. Finally, I would like to remind you, Mr. Thomas, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony in this court. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, when we adjourned yesterday, we were discussing the issue of Motorola radios. Do you recall whether on any occasion during the time you were assigned in Sarajevo, whether you saw any senior Bosnian Serb army officers carrying Motorola radios?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every senior commander on both sides had Motorolas

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you, Mr. Mundis, that you look at me. I am listening to the French channel and I will see whether the French translation is able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of information would the UNMOs be transmitting over the UN radio net?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would transmit --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I apologise, but this is an example, an important example. The question was, and I will repeat it: "What type of information... " And the translation which you heard, as I did, is: "Did those operators transmit it through the radio network?" And I don't think that is the question, and I think it is important here and I have to point it out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is corrected by your observation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question to you was, Mr. Thomas, whether -- what type of information the UNMOs would be transmitting over the UN radio net?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would transmit almost all information over the radio net that had any urgency to it. For example, if shelling was taking place, we would transmit this so that other people listening to our net would have the opportunity of being warned about the danger. If there was a sniper incident, we would also pass this immediately on the net, in particular, the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What language was used over the UN radio net at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language of the mission was English. On the lower levels of the contingent nets, I suspect that they used the language of that contingent, but I can't confirm this. I did hear French spoken on the French military net. But I must be clear, the language used at the higher levels, the official language was English, and that was used on the military observer net.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any type of -- was any type of code language employed on the UN radio net?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point -- at one point, we considered using a code, but as we knew other people from other UN agencies monitor our net, we wanted to send the locations, the map reference, grid references, in clear so that if shelling was occurring and we were reporting it, that they would understand where this shelling was happening and could be warned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The -- I take it from that answer, sir, that the information conveyed included very specific map references to the location of the shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I should add to that, in my training today, when I train military observers, I emphasise: Get the map reference first and the details follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, were there any instances that you recall in which you or others in your presence used the UN radio net specifically to address either of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say that we knew the warring parties listened to our net, both sides, and I used this knowledge that when I emerged from a meeting with either of the warring parties, I would broadcast to my teams what I understood had been agreed to at the meeting in English. And I assumed that this -- and I assumed that the warring parties would -- were listening, would hear this, and this committed them to the agreement as I understood it. And if they tried to come back and change it after, it made it more difficult for them to do that. And I found that this -- and I found that this procedure did work as they had more difficulty trying to tell me that something hadn't been said if I had already told all my people what I understood had been said. I assumed everything that I said on the radio in Sarajevo was heard by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown the document marked P2578.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the booth do have copies of these documents. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, can you identify the document that is now before you, P2578?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is a summary that we started preparing in March that I took with me to meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of information is contained in these summaries?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a summary of the major incidents, and you will see on the second page it has a summary of some of the matters that we were dealing with. Note the heading "Matters Resolved" and the heading "Matters Still Requiring Attention." And, of course, ignore the comments of my New Zealand duty operations officer on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I notice, for example, under the entry marked 5 March on the first page, the first entry under 5 March, there is reference to SA fire. Can you tell us what that acronym "SA" stands for, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The acronym stands for "small arms."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask the assistance of the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P2442.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, are you familiar with the document marked P2442, which is currently in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Although, to make it clear to the Court, this is actually a collection of various documents, not all from the same date and not all prepared at the same time by the same person. These are a collection of what I would call "intelligence documents." Some were prepared for me before I arrived to give me background. Some were items prepared for me at my request, such as the list of maps. And some are assessments prepared by the military observers I had working as military information officers or intelligence. In fact, the pages you see before you are out of order. This was in my intelligence binder in my office in Sarajevo, and this is a selection of documents from one of my four main binders that I always kept in my office. Is this sufficient detail for the Court? I can add more to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have a few specific questions for you, sir. If you see the stamped numbers towards the upper right-hand corner of these documents, I would ask that you turn to the page ending 750.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Beginning on page 750 and continuing through pages 760, there are a series of documents that contain names and what appear to be functional Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. titles. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what these documents are?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents -- these documents represent the briefing notes prepared for me when I arrived in Sector Sarajevo on 15 October, 1993. And before I would visit one of these headquarters, for example, General Galic's headquarters, I would be able to read this so that I would know who I was meeting and what their function was in that headquarters. The handwritten notes that you see are my notes. For example, I didn't meet all the brigade commanders. Some brigade commanders, I never met. Some brigades, I have a question mark beside. Is this sufficient detail for the Court? Would you require further edification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a couple of questions with respect to the acronyms appearing on page 750 in the centre column under the heading: "Function."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which acronym --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you would please go to the second line, it indicates "COS."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Next line, "DCOS"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: "DCO" on the following line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy Chief of Staff for discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Finally, toward the bottom of that list, "COO"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of Operations. Chief Operations Officer would be the correct English. Chief Operations Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be handed two exhibits, P2170 and P3706.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I would ask you first to turn your attention to P2170. As an initial matter, let me ask you if you read and understand the French language?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Canadian government level 4 for reading comprehension, which is more than functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe, please --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document prepared in French, talking about a shelling incident. Do you want to question me on the details?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you -- first let me ask you if you know or ever met either the drafter or the releasing officer of this document.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the drafter of this shelling report, which is document that ends 893, however, the officer that prepared the cover sheet, 892, was on the-- plans officer on the staff of Sector Sarajevo headquarters and I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you turn to the page ending -- if you turn to the page ending in the numbers 893, can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what this shelling report refers to.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shelling report refers to 120-millimetre impacts which killed six children. The author of the report tried to determine from the direction the angle of approach and other technical -- meteorological conditions, which direction the mortar rounds were fired from. So he makes a point that it was fired from the same mortar tube that was fired during a duration of several minutes, and it appears to be an additional conclusion by some kind of intelligence specialist saying that this mortar most likely was fired from either the Stup area of Sarajevo or from Ilidza, from the Serb side. Do you want me to elaborate further on the actual technical details?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I simply, sir, would ask if based on your experience whether the -- this appears to be a thorough and professional crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This appears to me to be about as thorough as it can be done under the circumstances. There never can be 100 per cent guarantee, but the French employed a specialist who did a very good job in this particular matter, and I would have accepted this report without question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask you now, Mr. Thomas, to turn to the document marked P3706. Is this document also a crater analysis report?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is in a slightly different format probably because the English format was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe -- can you describe what this report refers to, please?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report also refers to another mortar impacts, a series of mortar impacts at a different time. Let me just see if it -- it -- and obviously, there were four adults and three children killed in the description of the casualties, and it is trying to undertake again an analysis from which direction it was fired. However, the only conclusion is shown on page 899, in which he gives a direction. The mortar impact area from the map, as you can see, impacted in Dobrinja, and if you were to check -- if you were to check the grid references given, that would also be the general location, and he gives an approach which indicates it was fired from the Lukavica area. This report, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This report, again prepared by the same officer that prepared the previous report and also with the covering sheet by an officer that I knew in the headquarters, I would have accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions for the witness at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to start the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the question is whether we are ready to start, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have just told us just a minute ago, on the basis of the document that was given to you, the document stated that the firing was coming from Lukavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to give the witness the latest document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number is 3706.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I have to say that I didn't say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, please, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would you like to say, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated that the map showed that the shell originated in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to verify this, something, Mr. President. Just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The page that I referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if there is any need to ask the witness to stop answering, please address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when I am verifying the transcript, please see to it that the witness doesn't address anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Page 21, line 1, says: [In English] "He gives I think is the map, but I don't know." [Interpretation] I am reading, line 21, you declared: [In English] "Which indicates it was fired from the Lukavica area." Witness, just wait a minute, just listen to my question first. For what reason can you affirm what I have just read to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Lawyer, this is a map and there is nothing in there that is written that says the round was fired from Lukavica. However, if you look at your document, which I assume you have in front of you, you will see an arrow drawn to scale which shows, in a very technical manner, the direction of the approach of the round and the probable source of its origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I am interrupting you. We shall proceed. I am not trying to be discourteous, I am just trying to be efficient, and I ask you to stop when I ask you to stop. Can you understand me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, perhaps I should explain the following to you. If, for reasons of efficiency, the Defence counsel thinks that your answer was sufficient in relation to what he wanted to hear from you, he might interrupt you. If, however, there would ever be a situation where you feel that being stopped would distort or would not -- would distort the information you had given until then because you wanted to add something which might change what you had said before, then, please ask me whether you may continue your answer. And I will then decide on whether you are allowed to continue your answer or whether Defence counsel is entitled at that moment to ask you -- at that moment to ask a new question to you. May I also ask you to very carefully listen to the questions and perhaps not interfere when the question is still put to you. So wait until the full question has been put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Mr. President. And could I ask then if, in the opinion of the three of you, that you are very clear that I am referring to an indicator on a map and not to a written statement with reference to this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you clarified this now, at least. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to, also with the wish of respecting the time, to answer simply by a "yes" or "no" answer. Would this be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, that would depend on the question, but if you are able to answer by "yes" or "no" and if the question allows it, please do so. If, on the other hand, you think that a "yes" or "no" could not reflect your knowledge properly and that we would be mislead by just a "yes" or "no," then you could indicate so and ask whether you could elaborate what you said until then. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, first thing: Do you understand spoken French?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sufficient to make answers in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you are an artillery officer, are you not?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am a tank officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I apologise. You are a tank officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I suppose that you have a wide academic training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what you mean by "wide." I have a Masters degree in War Studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That is exactly what I had in mind, thank you very much, Witness. If tank officers are not directly interested in mortars, they nevertheless have some knowledge about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can elaborate further --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...firstly what next questions Mr. Piletta-Zanin has for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us if, in practice, it is difficult to determine on the basis of a crater analysis the range of a shot, what we call the range?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Range is not difficult to at all. A certain type of mortar will have a range capability and that is the easiest thing to determine. If you have a sample of the round, you know the range of that round and you can draw a radius with that range around the impact area and determine easily what falls within that range. The most difficult thing is direction because shrapnel, when it hits, it depends exactly on how the fuse hits, and the shrapnel pattern can change. Does this answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is an answer. It doesn't answer my question but it is an answer, nevertheless. Thank you. Witness, perhaps I did not express myself correctly. I am talking precisely not about the range of mortar, but the range of a specific shot, that is to say, on the basis of a mortar impact, can you, with accuracy, say that the shot came from 1.250 metres or 1.372 metres, let us say?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it always is difficult because there is a number of factors that enter into even the simplest of artillery rounds, such as weather, the wind, how the fuse hits. But all of the -- mortars are the easiest to determine the range because they have a fixed ammunition base. Artillery rounds, you vary the range by adding more or less cartridges. But the mortar rounds, 120-millimetre mortar rounds cannot fire beyond 4.000 metres, so then it is a process of elimination and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise. We are not talking about general range. Many people have spoken about range in general. I a speaking about the difference from a shot, let us say a shot "A." Is it true or not that it is particularly difficult on the basis of a crater analysis to determine the distance at which -- from which the shot was fired?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To pinpoint to exact location might be difficult because to determine how far the round was fired will depend on whether you can determine -- you know the general characteristics of the weapon, it would have been fired from a radius, within a radius of 4.000 metres at the impact area. So now you are arguing about whether it was at 2000 or 4.000. To determine that aspect, if the Court will let me elaborate further, it will depend on the trajectory because, for shorter ranges, you will fire higher and it will come down in a steeper trajectory. To get further out, you will have changed the elevation and it will come at a different trajectory, and that is where to say that it was 1500 or 2000 will be difficult because you must determine how it hit. But crater analysis actually helps in that because the point of impact of the round, as it comes into the ground like this, will determine a shrapnel pattern. If it is coming fairly straight, that is, it has been fired at short range, then it will come in and the fuse head will be embedded partly into the ground, depending on the nature of the ground - this is one of the complicating factors - and the shrapnel pattern will be different than if it is fired from a longer range and the round will come in a little bit less and maybe the bottom part of the round --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise for interrupting you. We have heard this from other witnesses. Can I conclude -- just listen to my question, wait for my question. Can I deduce from your technical explanation, interesting explanation, that what you call a fuse and sometimes refer to as the stabiliser is taken out before a statistical analysis, this could serious modify the results of such an analysis?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid this question is -- I don't understand the question because perhaps the incorrect terminology. The fuse is in the warhead, and when it hits, it is usually completely exploded. Whereas the fin, which is the stabilising part, may remain intact. It will tell very little because -- it is the pattern of the shrapnel that will give the indication. How did the fuse hit --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I spoke about -- and I apologise because I am not an expert in the matter, I spoke about, actually, what I had in mind is a fin, a stabilising element. If it is moved, this fin is moved, this stabilising element, before the analysis is made, and if it touches the crater, would this modify the conclusions of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, no. Because the shrapnel pattern indicates how the fuse exploded, as much as you can determine when it hit. And how the fuse hit determines the angle of the trajectory. The fin, for any one of a number of reasons, including the secondary explosion as the main content of the warhead explodes, could throw the fin away. Or if the fin -- the certain types of soil, the fin may become imbedded in the soil, or it could be moved by the explosion or by the sand or whatever debris fills back in. But I think that's the kind of question that even normal combat arms officers would argue over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to listen quite carefully to the question, because it was my understanding that the question was about if the tail-fin has been removed after the explosion, let us say by man, taken out or changed from position, whether that would affect the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I think not because the shrapnel pattern should remain intact. Only if the shrapnel pattern itself, when you yank this out, would that distort the conclusions. It could be a factor and I suggest then you -- if you have concrete examples, you ask one of the experts you call in later. And, in fact, you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We shall do it. We shall do it, thank you. But is it not true and can you answer "yes" or "no," if it is possible, is it not right that the in situ position of the stabilising element, the fin, is useful for determining the angle of descent, yes or no, in regard to the ground?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. I would attach more weight to have the fuse hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. I agree. Is it true that the angle of descent is a determining factor for determining the parabola?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I will ask you another series of questions and I will ask you to give me a "yes" or "no" answer. You spent a number of months in Sarajevo, more than a year; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent nine months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I apologise. So more or less, one year. Witness, I have read your statement. You mentioned that you tried to sleep one or two nights out of three in the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, which, in fact, means that you could move in and out of Sarajevo and on the Lima side, too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, when you used to move around Sarajevo, I suppose that you were not restricted to a single commune but that you would visit the entire sector of Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure what you mean by that question. If you mean -- if you are seeking me to say, "Yes, I had no restrictions," that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no, I am not trying to make you say anything but the truth. Were you restricted in your tours to certain areas of Sarajevo or to the large Sarajevo, the Greater Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, by both sides. I had to go, especially at night, go through one or two crossing points.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. But my question did not relate to the cross points but whether you, personally, could you have travelled in all parts of Sarajevo during your nine months, whatever side; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer isn't -- can't be answered by "yes" or "no" because it changed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I withdraw my question. Thank you. So depart from the principle that you were very familiar with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were parts of Sarajevo I was very familiar with and there were parts that I did not see at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But I am referring to the situation in Sarajevo, not the localisation. Is your answer "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I was familiar with the situation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, in your capacity as military observer, you stated, I believe, that you were very alert to what -- that the people under your orders were very accurate in reporting facts, either relating to shelling or relating to sniping incidents, or any other important events. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried to make them as accurate as we could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it true that you, yourself, as the person in charge, you placed importance on the fact that one should be as certain as possible to have the sit-rep reports reflect the realities to the greatest possible extent?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, you were able to visit -- to travel in Sarajevo with difficulty, and I would like to ask you the following questions: If you can answer "yes" or "no," I would be very grateful to you and I thank you in advance. Do you know what MUP was?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I don't understand the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: MUP, [In English] M-u-p.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the police organisation, is that correct? It is a synonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you know it, then just tell us: True, it is a police organisation.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to recall from -- I have been on another UN mission with different organisations. MUP, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know where the MUP was based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall where it was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which means that you used to know?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about police organisations, yes, I knew where there were several police organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am referring to headquarters, to the main office of the police, of the MUP, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew where the Sarajevo -- so-called Sarajevo police chief worked, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us where that was?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- well, I would do better with my map. But it was down -- it was in the centre of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You will possibly get my map later. But could you roughly tell us where it was?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the centre of town and it wasn't too far from the parliament buildings, and I went there at night, most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the word "La Benevolencija" mean anything to you? Witness, we will give you a map in a while. It is here and you will be able to orient yourself. But I would like to know, unless it is a good moment for making a break -- perhaps it would be a good moment

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just about to ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Thank you for assisting me. We will have a break until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We took a bit more time to consider all the issues raised in the beginning and we thought we could do it in 30 minutes, but it took us a few minutes more. As far as Witness W, because that is the most urgent one, and Witness Y is concerned, protective measures have been sought for them. The Chamber has not received a copy of the letters but just of the translations. We would like to receive copies of the letters - I take it that they are in French - will be provided to the Chamber this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, they have been translated. It was my decision to not include them because I did not think that they added anything, but I am more than happy to provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I do understand that it was your opinion that they didn't -- that they didn't add anything, but whether this is the translation of letters, we do not know, because we haven't seen the letters. But just on the assumption of the translation being a proper translation of the letters, the parties may expect the Chamber to decide next Monday that the protective measures requested will be granted. And if there would be any dispute as to whether Witness W and Witness Y could testify in this court, the Chamber is of the opinion that they can. The reason why I am saying this is since this issue has been raised in the response of the request for protective measures by the Defence. That is one issue. The second issue is about the schedule of next week. The Chamber could, in general terms, agree with this schedule as suggested by you, Mr. Ierace, but does not specifically express itself on Mr. Tucker and whether documents have been communicated in time. But as a starting point, your schedule suggested for next week is agreed upon by the Chamber. Then the third issue is the request of the Defence to have a break at 5.00 this afternoon. The Chamber expects the Defence to continue cross-examination up 'til where it can do so, and every minute we lose on this Friday, we will try to gain again next Monday. As I indicated to you, we are more flexible next Monday. That means that, if necessary, we would sit also in the afternoon, if all the arrangements can be made. But the courtroom is available. So the time you are not using today, Mr. Piletta-Zanin and Ms. Pilipovic, will be additionally scheduled for next Monday. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might I clarify something, because I think I may have misunderstood you. After I spoke a few minutes ago, you referred to the need to check the accuracy of the translations. Two days ago, on the 29th of May, we did file the original French request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't seen them. If they have been filed and if by any mistake, it has not reached the Chamber, then, of course, if they are filed, you don't have to provide a second copy of the letters. That goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I was referring simply to the covering letters which accompanied the formal request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The request we received, we had one annex and the annex consisted of two documents, in English, saying at the bottom line that it was a letter of the French embassy dated the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] True.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the annexes in French that have been filed on the 29th of May would be the originals, I also know that "note verbale" are usually not signed, but it gives us no clue as to establish that these documents, although in French, originate from the French embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, and this afternoon I will file, or if you prefer, simply hand up, to save time, photocopies of those original documents and I anticipate you will then see that what has been annexed is, in fact, what was received. But full documentation will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ierace. So those documents that are -- these documents come from the French embassy, these requests, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. There was an accompanying letter, which I think will make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think though there have been a "note verbale," a front page, and then the second page -- well, we will see what we are provided with. So I think all the urgent matters have been dealt with by now. May I ask the usher to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we are following this procedure, I think we could continue. I think there is a decision which is pending with regard to Article 73. I think you remember we asked for your Trial Chamber to take a decision. I don't know if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...I signed half an hour ago a document which gives in writing the reasons for the decisions -- for the decision to -- already orally given on the 22nd of May, that the Prosecutor was entitled to add Witness AD to the list. We did not take a decision yet on your request to -- but if having seen the decision, the reasons in writing, if this would cause you to add anything to the reasons you brought to the attention of the Chamber, why you would like to appeal against that decision, an opportunity will be given to that and then we will decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be very grateful to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Two matters, very quickly. At page 35, line 4, there was an inadvertent mention of the name of one of the witnesses for whom protective measures have been sought, so perhaps that could be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And secondly, at the appropriate stage, I wish to be heard as to the appropriateness of issuing a certificate. On the last occasion that a certificate was sought, it might be said the Prosecution took a fairly neutral stance. That would not be the case this time. We would strongly oppose the issue of a certificate in respect of your decision on Witness AD. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would like to have at least an opportunity to have oral argument, even if it would be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we took notice of that, Mr. Ierace. I will take care that the reasons given for the decision in respect of Witness AD will be distributed among the parties, even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Ierace, please check on page 35 - it is not in my recollection any more - would it be true that on page 35, line 2, the name was mentioned because on line 4, I see a name, but that is not a protected name. At the very end of the line, 35.2, I think there it might have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would we have line 4, the name of a UN official is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, I don't think it was line 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please locate precisely, but immediately, so that -- we have only limited time to make redactions, and if you would please inform Madam Registrar immediately. Perhaps, meanwhile, we could ask the usher already to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript has not caught it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, of course it is on the audio tape and the videotape. If you could just try to find out where it has been because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to save time, I will ask for the maps to be distributed while Mr. Ierace is trying to find this part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...as usual, procedural issues that you know is the favorite sport of all the lawyers in courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we think it is around page 35, line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 35 line 11, let me just have a look. I think for certainty, perhaps, the issues discussed are not such that it would affect the public character of this trial, so, therefore, I would rather be a bit more liberal in redacting the statement. If we start at 35, line 1, and if you would stop at 16, wouldn't that be the most safe way of dealing with it? And if there is any need to reduce the redaction, we always could do it later on. Madam Registrar, page 35, line 1 to 16, yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know if there is a sufficient number of maps for everyone, but I think so. Witness, we are going to carry on. I have provided you with a map. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would appreciate it if you could approach the microphone. It is not for me, it is to facilitate the task of the interpreters. Thank you very much. Witness, would you like me to address you by a rank? I will do that willingly.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, can you recognise the map that you have on your right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the map that I use, but I recognise the map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we are going to use this map in a minute. For the moment, I would like you to answer by "yes" or "no" to the extent that this is possible and answer the questions that I am going to ask you. We stopped with the subject of the MUP during the break and you said that you knew that this was a police institution. My questions are as follows, Witness: Witness, do you know where the Gras, G-r-a-s, building is located or what one calls the Gras building?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I if I could elaborate to the Court, I would like to explain why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I don't think that is necessary if you don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it's enough, Mr. Thomas, that no one expects any knowledge which you do not have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, if I could explain to the Chairman, at these places at night, we didn't -- we went to see a commander or a person in a location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, you don't know so that is accepted by everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I apologise, but if you could answer by saying "yes" or "no," please do so. The same question for Petar Dakic.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name means nothing at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say, "at this time," do you mean to say that it meant something before?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I can't recall the name. If I had known it was going to be raised in Court, I would have looked up in my notes, and maybe I had dealings with that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Witness, Kulin Ban, is this a name that means something to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means nothing to me at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Does the name of Stela in relation to Sarajevo mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This name means nothing at these times -- this time and we are not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I didn't ask how you operated - we are wasting time - and your answer is not very agreeable, and I am allowing myself to say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you were asked whether a name rings a bell, we will easily accept that it does or does not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just make a comment though?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could say it in one or two words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to locations to meet people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you are explaining why. If you don't know something, it needs no explanation. You just don't know. Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you, Witness. Witness, does the name Pavle Goranin mean anything to you; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, does the name of Valter Peric mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, does the name Magros mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, does the name Zica, Z-i-t-s, with a diacritic mark on top, "a," does this mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Diacritic mark, that term is not understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It is not important. Does the name that you heard mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, does the name Kobra in relation to Sarajevo mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you therefore didn't know that the group Kobra was a paramilitary group in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I knew a paramilitary group by the name of Kobra --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Answer "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name of the Ljiljan group mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, does the name Drago Prazina mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, does the name Fatih mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you elaborate or how a relationship I might have had --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In relation to Sarajevo, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Does the name Sultan Fatih mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you were holding a post in Sarajevo. Can you remind us how many brigades during the period of your stay there, how many brigades were there in Sarajevo? Were there 10 brigades?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number changed because one brigade was dissolved. I would say there was nine when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer, Witness. Witness, are you in a position to know where, for example, the CC, the command and control, of the 102nd Motorised Brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a position to know. My LO would take me to that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I am asking you, as a witness, did you know where it was located?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, I knew where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if the witness says that he knew it in 1993, the next question, although it might already have been answered, would be whether he knows now. As a matter of fact, I understood his answer as, "I don't know now but I knew it at that time" and it is of no use asking where it was located if he does not know at this very moment. So would you please then clarify that? And may I take it that when you are talking about the 10 brigades in Sarajevo, that you are referring to one of the parties in the conflict? It was not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, necessarily, Mr. President, when I talk about the 10 brigades, and I did specify that it was in Sarajevo, in the town itself. In fact, there are two sites since we know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...understanding was well since it was neither --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Very well. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I have understood you correctly, you no longer know today, you can no longer remember where the command of the 102nd Brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have been on another operation since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am not questioning your memory. I am trying, like everyone else, to find out what the truth is, that is all. And I am certain that you are going to help us to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you refrain from commenting. If there is any guidance you would like to give to the witness, would you please ask me and suggest for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, willingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, as a result, did you know in which building this command was located?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure, in 1993, I did know. I know that I might have been at a meeting there, but I can't recall now at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Thank you very much. Witness, I am going to -- with the assistance of the usher, a document which bears the number 113, D113. It is a document that has been provided by the Prosecution. I will wait for you to be provided with this document before continuing with my series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have one more document available, if necessary. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, can you recognise this type of document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a similar document in my intelligence binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, could you please have a look at page 2, the one which finishes with the numbers 5 and 7. Have you got that page?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Do you know where the command post of the 101st Brigade was located and with regard to the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not clear on your question. The third paragraph? "It is estimated that the Bosnians," is that the paragraph in question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no. Perhaps you don't have the right page in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In that case, when I said "paragraph," I mean the paragraphs which include, first of all, a list of brigades, and then they have names in front of it. This is what I consider to be paragraphs one, two, three. I am going to ask my question again, Witness. Can you see the 101st Brigade in front of you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know where the command and control post of the 101st Brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. In order to save time, Witness, I would be grateful if you could do the following: Can you read the entire third paragraph, that is to say, the names that we have marked, and if you know of one of these brigades and where its precise location was with regard to the headquarters, I would be very grateful if you could let us know this. Could you do that? And could the interpreters please have a copy, if there is a copy available. The English booth has asked me for a copy, and for the B/C/S and French booths, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you have two additional copies, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Unfortunately not, not at the moment, but we could try to do some copies later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give you a quick answer. At this time, without my own personal map which I carried in Sarajevo, I cannot point out on any map that you have provided me with the exact locations. If I can tell you that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, the question was whether you could -- whether you would know at this time. The answer is, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, thank you for this answer. Witness, I am going to ask you the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if we have any technical problems, Mr. President. I don't think that we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to wait for a while, since the French court reporter doesn't receive any text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French booth is not working presently, Mr. President. For some reason, the console is not responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to wait until the French court reporter --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is not responding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
